issue: Does Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2 validly expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses such as conspiracy, attempt, and aiding and abetting, or is the commentary inconsistent with the guideline's text and therefore unenforceable after Kisor v. Wilkie?

sides.position: Application Note 1 improperly expands 'controlled substance offense' beyond the text of § 4B1.2(b), which omits inchoate offenses. The commentary is not entitled to deference on this point, and the guideline's detailed definition excludes conspiracy and attempt (expressio unius).
cases: United States v. Winstead, 890 F.3d 1082 (D.C. Cir. 2018)
United States v. Havis, 927 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2019) (en banc)
United States v. Castillo, 69 F.4th 648 (9th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: Application Note 1 validly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include aiding and abetting, conspiracy, and attempt, and the commentary is consistent with the guideline and entitled to deference.
cases: United States v. Vea-Gonzales, 999 F.2d 1326 (9th Cir. 1993)
United States v. Crum, 934 F.3d 963 (9th Cir. 2019)

this_court: Application Note 1 improperly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b), so the court sides with the D.C. and Sixth Circuits and rejects its own prior deference holdings in Vea-Gonzales and Crum.
quote: In short, we must decide which side of a growing intercircuit split is correct on the question whether Application Note 1 improperly expands the definition of “controlled substance offense” in § 4B1.2(b).
cite: United States v. Roberto Castillo, 69 F.4th 648 (9th Cir. 2023)
